stem: A company needs a managed relational database for its order system that runs MySQL.

options.why: DynamoDB is a NoSQL key-value and document database.
Neptune is a graph database, so it doesn't meet this requirement.
RDS provides managed relational databases, including MySQL.
ElastiCache is an in-memory cache, which isn't what this scenario needs.

explanation.answer: Amazon RDS makes it easy to set up, operate and scale relational databases such as MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server and Db2.
explanation.concept: RDS automates backups, patching and Multi-AZ failover.

stem: A company wants a MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible database with higher performance and storage that grows automatically across three AZs.

options.why: DynamoDB is NoSQL, which isn't what this scenario needs.
DocumentDB is a document database compatible with MongoDB.
Redshift is a data warehouse for analytics.
Aurora is MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible, with high performance and storage replicated across three AZs.

explanation.answer: Amazon Aurora is a relational database engine compatible with MySQL and PostgreSQL, with storage that automatically grows and is replicated six ways across three AZs.
explanation.concept: Aurora Serverless scales capacity automatically.

stem: A gaming company needs a NoSQL database with single-digit millisecond performance at any scale and no servers to manage.

options.why: DynamoDB is a serverless NoSQL key-value and document database with consistent low latency.
Neptune is a graph database, so it doesn't meet this requirement.
Redshift is for analytics, so it doesn't meet this requirement.
RDS is relational and requires instance sizing.

explanation.answer: Amazon DynamoDB is a fully managed, serverless NoSQL database that delivers single-digit millisecond performance at any scale.
explanation.concept: DynamoDB offers on-demand and provisioned capacity modes.
explanation.examTip: Serverless NoSQL, ms latency, any scale = DynamoDB.

stem: A company wants to run complex SQL analytics queries over petabytes of historical sales data.

options.why: ElastiCache is an in-memory cache, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.
Redshift is a petabyte-scale data warehouse for SQL analytics.
DynamoDB is optimized for key-value access, not complex analytics.
RDS is designed for transactional workloads, not petabyte analytics.

explanation.answer: Amazon Redshift is a fully managed data warehouse that uses columnar storage and parallel processing for fast analytics on large datasets.
explanation.concept: OLTP (transactions) → RDS/Aurora/DynamoDB. OLAP (analytics) → Redshift.
explanation.examTip: Data warehouse / analytics at scale = Redshift.

stem: An application repeatedly reads the same data from its database and wants microsecond response times.

options.why: Redshift is for analytics, which isn't what this scenario needs.
Streams capture item changes; they don't cache reads.
ElastiCache provides in-memory caching with Redis OSS, Valkey or Memcached.
Replicas offload reads but are still disk-based databases, not microsecond caches.

explanation.answer: Amazon ElastiCache is a managed in-memory data store that speeds up applications by caching frequently accessed data.
explanation.concept: Caching reduces database load and latency.

stem: A social network wants to store and query relationships between users, such as friends of friends.

options.why: Redshift is a data warehouse, which isn't what this scenario needs.
Relational databases handle deep relationship traversals less efficiently.
Timestream is a time series database, which isn't what this scenario needs.
Neptune is a graph database for highly connected data.

explanation.answer: Amazon Neptune is a managed graph database for applications that work with highly connected datasets, such as social networks and fraud detection.
explanation.concept: Graph databases store relationships as first-class data.

stem: A company runs MongoDB workloads and wants a managed, MongoDB-compatible document database on AWS.

options.why: DocumentDB is a managed document database compatible with MongoDB APIs.
Keyspaces is compatible with Apache Cassandra.
Aurora is relational, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.
Neptune is a graph database, which isn't what this scenario needs.

explanation.answer: Amazon DocumentDB is a fully managed document database that supports MongoDB workloads.
explanation.concept: Match the database to the data model and existing tools.

stem: A company needs its Amazon RDS database to fail over automatically if the primary database's AZ goes down.

options.why: That replicates S3 objects, not RDS databases.
Multi-AZ keeps a standby in another AZ and fails over automatically.
Size doesn't add AZ redundancy, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

options.text: Read replicas in the same AZ
options.why: Replicas in the same AZ fail with it, and read replicas don't fail over automatically by default.

explanation.answer: RDS Multi-AZ deployments maintain a synchronous standby in a different AZ with automatic failover.
explanation.concept: Read replicas are mainly for scaling reads.
explanation.examTip: Automatic DB failover across AZs = Multi-AZ. Read scaling = read replicas.

stem: An RDS database is overloaded by reporting queries that only read data.
prompt: Which feature helps offload the read traffic?

options.why: Lifecycle rules manage S3 objects, which isn't what this scenario needs.
The Multi-AZ standby isn't used to serve reads in a standard Multi-AZ instance deployment.
Read replicas serve read-only traffic, reducing load on the primary.
Backups protect data; they don't serve reads.

explanation.answer: Read replicas let you scale read-heavy workloads by directing read queries to one or more copies of the database.
explanation.concept: Replicas use asynchronous replication.

references.title: Working with DB instance read replicas

stem: A company is choosing databases for three needs: customer orders with strict transactions, a product catalog with flexible attributes at huge scale, and session caching.

options.text: ElastiCache for orders, Aurora for the catalog, DynamoDB for sessions
options.why: A cache isn't a durable system of record for orders.
Neptune is designed for graph data, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: DynamoDB for orders, Redshift for the catalog, S3 for sessions
options.why: Redshift isn't a catalog store and S3 isn't a session cache.

options.text: Aurora for orders, DynamoDB for the catalog, ElastiCache for sessions
options.why: Each service matches its data access pattern.

explanation.answer: Relational databases (Aurora, RDS) suit transactional data. DynamoDB suits flexible, massive-scale key-value data. ElastiCache suits caching.
explanation.concept: Purpose-built databases: pick the engine that fits each workload.

stem: A startup's DynamoDB traffic is unpredictable, with long quiet periods and sudden spikes.

options.why: On-demand charges per request and handles spikes without capacity planning.
Changing databases isn't needed for this.

options.text: Provisioned capacity set for the peak
options.why: This pays for peak capacity even when idle.
Reservations suit steady, predictable usage.

explanation.answer: DynamoDB on-demand capacity serves requests without capacity planning and charges per read and write request.
explanation.concept: Provisioned mode with auto scaling can be cheaper for steady, predictable traffic.

stem: A company wants a relational database but doesn't want to manage OS patching, backups or replication.

options.text: Install MySQL on an EC2 instance
options.why: This keeps OS and database management with the company.
RDS automates patching, backups and replication.
EBS is storage, not a database, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: Use AWS Lambda to store data
options.why: Lambda runs code; it isn't a database, which isn't what this scenario needs.

explanation.answer: Amazon RDS handles routine database tasks so teams can focus on applications.
explanation.concept: Self-managed databases on EC2 offer more control but more work.

stem: A company runs Apache Cassandra on premises and wants a serverless, Cassandra-compatible database on AWS without managing clusters.

options.why: Redshift is a data warehouse, so it doesn't meet this requirement.
DocumentDB is compatible with MongoDB, not Cassandra.
Keyspaces is a serverless, Cassandra-compatible database service.
Neptune is a graph database, which isn't what this scenario needs.

explanation.answer: Amazon Keyspaces is a scalable, serverless, managed database compatible with Apache Cassandra, so existing Cassandra code and tools keep working.
explanation.concept: Pick the managed service that's compatible with the engine you already use.

stem: A company's internal app uses a relational database only a few hours per week and wants to avoid paying for idle database capacity.

options.text: A large provisioned RDS instance running 24/7
options.why: Capacity running 24/7 costs money when idle.
Redshift is a data warehouse, which isn't what this scenario needs.
ElastiCache is a cache, not a relational database.
Aurora Serverless scales capacity with demand, reducing cost when usage is low.

explanation.answer: Amazon Aurora Serverless automatically scales database capacity based on application demand.
explanation.concept: It suits intermittent, unpredictable or variable workloads.

stem: A team is learning AWS database services.
prompt: Which TWO statements are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Amazon Neptune is a data warehouse
options.why: Neptune is a graph database, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: Amazon Aurora is a relational database
options.why: Aurora is MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible relational.

options.text: Amazon DynamoDB is a NoSQL database
options.why: DynamoDB is a key-value and document NoSQL database.

options.text: Amazon Redshift is an in-memory cache
options.why: Redshift is a data warehouse, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: Amazon ElastiCache is a graph database
options.why: ElastiCache is an in-memory store, which isn't what this scenario needs.

explanation.answer: DynamoDB = NoSQL. Aurora/RDS = relational. Redshift = data warehouse. ElastiCache = cache. Neptune = graph.
explanation.concept: Purpose-built databases match data models.
explanation.examTip: Memorize one word per database service.

stem: A company wants to restore its RDS database to how it looked five minutes before a bad data change.

options.why: Automated backups allow restoring to any second within the retention period.
The standby is synchronous, so it contains the bad change too.

options.text: RDS read replicas promoted after the change
options.why: Replicas copy the bad change too, so it doesn't fit this scenario.
Alarms notify; they don't restore data, which isn't what this scenario needs.

explanation.answer: RDS automated backups enable point-in-time recovery to any second during the retention period, typically up to the last five minutes.
explanation.concept: Manual snapshots can also be kept as long as needed.
explanation.examTip: Restore to a specific moment = point-in-time recovery.

stem: A global app needs a DynamoDB table that users in Europe and Asia can read and write locally with low latency.

options.why: DAX caches reads in one Region; it doesn't replicate writes globally.
Global tables replicate data across Regions with local reads and writes.
Those are for RDS, not DynamoDB, so it doesn't meet this requirement.
That replicates S3 objects, which isn't what this scenario needs.

explanation.answer: DynamoDB global tables provide fully managed, multi-Region, multi-active replication.
explanation.concept: Each Region can serve reads and writes locally.

stem: A DynamoDB-based shopping site needs microsecond read latency for its most popular items.

options.why: Redshift is for analytics, which isn't what this scenario needs.
These apply to RDS, which isn't what this scenario needs.
DAX is an in-memory cache for DynamoDB that delivers microsecond reads.
Glue is for ETL, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

explanation.answer: Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is a fully managed in-memory cache for DynamoDB that improves read performance up to 10x.
explanation.concept: DAX is API-compatible with DynamoDB.

stem: An analyst asks which type of database suits running a few complex queries over years of data, rather than many small transactions.

options.why: Caches speed up repeated reads, so it doesn't meet this requirement.
OLTP handles many small, fast transactions.
Graph databases handle relationships, so it doesn't meet this requirement.
Data warehouses are built for complex analytical queries over large datasets.

explanation.answer: Online analytical processing (OLAP) systems like Amazon Redshift are designed for complex queries across large historical datasets.
explanation.concept: OLTP systems like Amazon RDS handle day-to-day transactions.

stem: A company needs a Redis-compatible in-memory database that is durable enough to be the primary database, not just a cache.

options.why: MemoryDB is a durable, Redis OSS- and Valkey-compatible in-memory database.
DAX is a cache in front of DynamoDB, not a Redis-compatible in-memory database.
Memcached is a cache without durability.
Redshift is a data warehouse, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

explanation.answer: Amazon MemoryDB is a durable in-memory database with Multi-AZ durability, suitable as a primary database.
explanation.concept: ElastiCache is primarily a cache; MemoryDB is a durable primary store.

stem: A company runs Microsoft SQL Server and wants to move it to a managed service on AWS without changing database engines.

options.why: DynamoDB is NoSQL and would require a redesign.
RDS supports SQL Server as a managed engine.
Timestream is for time series data, which isn't what this scenario needs.
Neptune is a graph database, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

explanation.answer: Amazon RDS supports Microsoft SQL Server, Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB and Db2 as managed engines.
explanation.concept: Same-engine moves are simpler than engine changes.

stem: A company wants continuous backups of a DynamoDB table so it can restore to any second in the last 35 days.

options.why: DAX is a cache, which isn't what this scenario needs.
Streams capture item changes but aren't a backup feature.
PITR provides continuous backups with restore to any second in up to 35 days.
Global tables replicate data across Regions, including mistakes.

explanation.answer: DynamoDB point-in-time recovery provides continuous backups, letting you restore to any second within the recovery window.
explanation.concept: On-demand backups and AWS Backup can also protect tables.
explanation.examTip: Restore DynamoDB to any second = PITR.

stem: An analytics team runs warehouse queries a few times a week and doesn't want to manage clusters.

options.why: RDS is for transactional workloads, which isn't what this scenario needs.
This charges for capacity when idle, which isn't what this scenario needs.
ElastiCache is a cache, so it doesn't meet this requirement.
Redshift Serverless runs analytics without managing clusters and charges for usage.

explanation.answer: Amazon Redshift Serverless automatically provisions and scales warehouse capacity and charges only when queries run.
explanation.concept: Serverless options exist across databases and analytics.
explanation.examTip: Occasional warehouse queries, no clusters = Redshift Serverless.

stem: A team wants to know which databases AWS fully manages so they don't need to choose instance sizes at all.
prompt: Which TWO services are serverless databases? (Select TWO.)

options.why: Aurora Serverless scales capacity automatically without instance sizing.
DynamoDB is serverless with no instances to size.

options.text: Amazon RDS for Oracle with a fixed instance class
options.why: This requires choosing instance sizes, which isn't what this scenario needs.
Node-based clusters require sizing, which isn't what this scenario needs.
This requires managing servers, which isn't what this scenario needs.

explanation.answer: DynamoDB and Aurora Serverless remove the need to provision database instances.
explanation.concept: ElastiCache and Redshift also offer serverless options.
explanation.examTip: Serverless databases: DynamoDB, Aurora Serverless (and more).

stem: A company wants to continuously replicate data from an on-premises PostgreSQL database to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL.

options.why: DMS supports full load and ongoing replication (change data capture).
Snowball moves data offline, not continuous replication.
Athena queries data in S3, so it doesn't meet this requirement.
QuickSight builds dashboards, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

explanation.answer: AWS DMS can perform a full load and then continuously replicate changes from the source database to the target.
explanation.concept: This keeps downtime minimal during cutover.
explanation.examTip: Ongoing DB replication to AWS = DMS.

references.title: What is AWS Database Migration Service?
